design_detail: Editorial (two pages) in Addiction by three researchers of the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, Sydney, arguing that opioid withdrawal can be fatal when its complications go untreated, and calling for medical withdrawal management or substitution treatment in custody. Evidence offered: the withdrawal syndrome as described in DSM-5; one UK death in custody (1998) known from a European Court of Human Rights case; ten deaths during opioid withdrawal in US jails reported in the press in 2013–2016, listed in a supporting appendix (Appendix S1, not read); a survey of US jail detoxification services; and studies of substitution treatment in custody. No search method, no denominators.
can_establish: That deaths during opioid withdrawal have been documented, all of them in custody, and the mechanism the authors propose: dehydration and raised blood sodium from untreated vomiting and diarrhoea, leading to heart failure.
cannot_establish: How often opioid withdrawal is fatal, whether such deaths are increasing, or the risk outside custody: there is no systematic case finding and no denominator, and the cases come from press reports and a court case.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (editorial). Cases: one UK death in custody in 1998, described from a casebook on the European Convention on Human Rights (ref. 3), and ten deaths in US jails reported in the public press between 2013 and 2016 that the authors were aware of (six women, four men, aged 18 to 49), listed in Appendix S1 (p. 199).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria or search method stated.
sample.selection_effects: Cases known through litigation and press coverage; deaths that were not reported, or not attributed to withdrawal, are missed, and no denominator of people going through withdrawal in custody is given.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; opioid withdrawal in custody as described in press and legal reports.

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history, other drugs (including alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal) and the cause-of-death findings of the reported cases are not described in the editorial.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; causes of death as reported (the UK case: hypoxic brain damage caused by cardiac arrest).
outcomes.operationalization: Death during opioid withdrawal in custody.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Counts only: 10 press-reported deaths in US jails, 2013–2016 (6 women, 4 men, aged 18 to 49), and 1 UK death (1998). Second-hand figures: only a quarter of US jails in one survey had alcohol or drug detoxification services (Fiscella et al., 2004, ref. 4); continued maintenance treatment associated with a 93% reduction in the risk of death in custody over a 10-year period (attributed to ref. 10).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only fatal cases in custody are presented; how often such deaths occur among people withdrawing from opioids is not addressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Documented deaths during opioid withdrawal, all in custodial settings, reported through a court case and the press, with a plausible mechanism (dehydration, raised blood sodium and heart failure after untreated vomiting and diarrhoea).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The editorial states that all such deaths are preventable with appropriate medical management and that in each case the process of dying appeared prolonged, with ample time to treat (p. 199); the case details are in an appendix. It speaks of a rising number of withdrawal deaths in US jails (p. 200) without trend data or denominators, and calls death an uncommon outcome without giving a rate.

timeline.event: A woman in custody in the UK went into heroin withdrawal with persistent vomiting, sudden weight loss and dehydration and died of hypoxic brain damage after cardiac arrest; a failure of duty of care was argued successfully before the European Court of Human Rights (as described, p. 199).
Fiscella et al.: survey of alcohol and opiate withdrawal in US jails; only a quarter had alcohol or drug detoxification services (as cited, ref. 4).
First of ten deaths during opioid withdrawal in US jails reported in the press between 2013 and 2016 (Appendix S1, not read).
Larney et al.: retrospective cohort study of opioid substitution therapy as a strategy to reduce deaths in prison (ref. 9; co-authored by two of the editorial's authors).
Rich et al.: randomised open-label trial of methadone continuation versus forced withdrawal on incarceration in a combined US prison and jail (ref. 10; Larney is a co-author).

replication.where_it_stands: An opinion piece establishing that fatal outcomes of opioid withdrawal are documented, in custody and with untreated dehydration, but giving no rate. How often withdrawal is fatal remains unanswered in the sources read. The 93% figure should be checked in its source before use, because its description fits the title of reference 9 rather than reference 10, to which it is attributed.

funding.funder: No funding stated for the editorial. Acknowledgement: the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre at the University of New South Wales is supported by funding from the Australian Government (p. 200).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, Sydney. Two of the ten references (refs 9 and 10), which carry the argument for substitution treatment in custody, are co-authored by Larney (both) and Farrell (ref. 9). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Systematic surveillance of deaths in custody, with a standardized cause-of-death review that identifies withdrawal-related deaths and the number of people entering custody dependent on opioids as the denominator, to give rates and trends; and a comparison of facilities with and without medical withdrawal management or substitution treatment.

domains.note: The cases are those the authors were aware of from press reports and a court case; no search method.
Neither the reliability of the press reports nor the cited studies are appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two of the ten references, which carry the substitution-treatment argument, are co-authored by the editorial's authors.
That every case was preventable, and that the number of deaths is rising, are asserted without data in the text.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how often opioid withdrawal is fatal
domains.note: Only fatal cases in custody are shown, with no denominator; the editorial does say that death is uncommon.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an editorial (METHODS §5.3). The piece is useful for the documented fact that people have died during untreated opioid withdrawal in custody and for the proposed mechanism; its figures are second-hand and its cases unsystematically gathered. Cite it for the existence and circumstances of such deaths, never for their frequency or trend.

key_findings.finding: Opioid withdrawal is generally characterized as a flu-like illness, subjectively severe but objectively mild, in contrast with the life-threatening alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal syndromes; the editorial argues that death, though uncommon, does occur and that complications of withdrawal are often underestimated and monitored inadequately.
key_findings.locator: Opening summary (left column, top); 1st paragraph ('Death is an uncommon, but catastrophic, outcome…'); 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Signs and symptoms listed: dysphoria, insomnia, dilated pupils, gooseflesh (piloerection), yawning, muscle aches, tearing, runny nose, nausea, fever, sweating, vomiting and diarrhoea; for short-acting opioids such as heroin, severity typically peaks at around 2 to 3 days.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph ('The opioid withdrawal syndrome is well-delineated…'), left column

key_findings.finding: Proposed mechanism of death: persistent vomiting and diarrhoea, if untreated, can lead to dehydration, hypernatraemia (raised blood sodium) and resulting heart failure.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph ('How could someone die during opiate withdrawal?'), left column

key_findings.finding: Documented deaths during the withdrawal process are all in jail settings and date back to the late 1990s: in 1998 a woman in custody in the UK went into heroin withdrawal with persistent vomiting, sudden weight loss and dehydration, and died of hypoxic brain damage caused by cardiac arrest; a failure of duty of care was argued successfully before the European Court of Human Rights.
The authors were aware of 10 similar deaths in US jails reported in the public press between 2013 and 2016: six women and four men, aged 18 to 49 years.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph, left column (cases listed in Appendix S1)
key_findings.note: Appendix S1 was not among the files read; the cases come from press reports, not from a systematic search.

key_findings.finding: The authors judge all such deaths preventable with appropriate medical management: in each case the process of dying appeared prolonged, with ample time to treat successfully. They describe the deaths as cases of neglect or lack of medical resources, note that intravenous rehydration is not regarded as appropriate outside health-care settings, and point to a failure to recognize serious dehydration.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph ('All such deaths are preventable…'), left column, continuing at the top of the right column

key_findings.finding: Jails process more drug withdrawals than any other single institution but often lack medical resources; one study of US jails found that only a quarter had alcohol or drug detoxification services (Fiscella et al., 2004).

Substitution treatment for people dependent on opioids entering custody is described as associated with lower mortality and better outcomes after release than enforced withdrawal; one study is cited for a 93% reduction in the risk of death in custody over a 10-year period with continued maintenance treatment.
key_findings.locator: 7th paragraph ('An alternative to withdrawal…'), right column
key_findings.note: The 93% figure is attributed to ref. 10, titled as a randomised trial of methadone continuation versus forced withdrawal on incarceration; its description (deaths in custody over 10 years) fits the title of ref. 9, a retrospective cohort study of substitution therapy and deaths in prison. Check the source before citing the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The 93% reduction in deaths in custody is attributed to ref. 10 (a randomised trial of methadone continuation versus forced withdrawal), whereas the description matches the title of ref. 9 (a retrospective cohort study of substitution therapy and deaths in prison).
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible citation slip; the figure cannot be cited from the editorial and should be taken from the primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence on how many people in prison use opiates is garbled ('comprise more than a substantial proportion prison populations') and gives no figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: No proportion can be cited from here.

reporting_issues.issue: The editorial refers to a rising number of deaths from withdrawal in US jails, but presents only cases from 2013–2016, with no earlier counts and no denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: A trend cannot be cited from this source.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), pp. 199–200 (all pages, checked on rendered pages at 150 dpi; the supporting information, Appendix S1 listing the reported deaths in custody, was not among the files and was not read)
